cities.name: New Whiteland
cities.school_district: Clark-Pleasant Community School Corporation (Whiteland Community High School)
cities.commute: New Whiteland is about 25 to 30 minutes from downtown Indianapolis (roughly 20 miles south), with US-31 running directly through town and I-65 reached at the Whiteland interchange just east.
cities.character: New Whiteland is a small suburban town in Pleasant Township that got its start in the 1950s when US-31 was rerouted through the area, incorporating in 1954. It sits immediately next to Whiteland and shares the Clark-Pleasant Community School Corporation, whose Whiteland Community High School (the Warriors) anchors the community. Housing runs from mid-century ranches near the older town core to newer subdivisions filling in along the fast-growing southern Indianapolis and Greenwood corridor.
highlights: Quick US-31 and I-65 access to Indianapolis
Generally more affordable than the Greenwood core
Clark-Pleasant schools and Whiteland Community High School

cities.name: Ingalls
cities.school_district: South Madison Community School Corporation (Pendleton Heights High School)
cities.commute: Ingalls is about 35 minutes from downtown Indianapolis (roughly 26 miles) via I-69, with Anderson about 12 miles northeast.
cities.character: Ingalls sits in the southwest corner of Madison County in Green Township, platted in 1893 and named for railroad official Melville E. Ingalls, with Fall Creek winding through the north side of town. It has been one of the area's faster-growing small towns as an I-69 commuter suburb, and it feeds the well-regarded South Madison Community Schools and Pendleton Heights High School. Buyers find a mix of newer subdivisions alongside older homes in the original town core.
highlights: Easy I-69 commute to Indianapolis and Anderson
Growing with newer subdivisions
South Madison / Pendleton Heights schools

cities.name: Chesterfield
cities.school_district: Anderson Community School Corporation (with the Delaware County / Salem Township edge in Daleville Community Schools)
cities.commute: Chesterfield is an Anderson- and Muncie-oriented town, about 50 minutes (roughly 44 miles) from downtown Indianapolis via I-69, with Anderson just minutes west and Muncie about 13 miles northeast.
cities.character: Chesterfield straddles Madison and Delaware counties along the White River, between Anderson to the west and Daleville to the east. It was first platted as 'West Union' in 1830, renamed in 1834, and incorporated in 1858. The town is nationally known for Camp Chesterfield, a historic spiritualist retreat listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Part of the Anderson metro area, it offers an established, affordable housing stock and a small-town setting.
highlights: Affordable, established housing
Historic Camp Chesterfield spiritualist heritage
Quick I-69 access at the SR-67 interchange, minutes from Anderson

cities.name: Frankton
cities.school_district: Frankton-Lapel Community Schools (Frankton Junior-Senior High School)
cities.commute: Frankton is a quiet northern Madison County town about 12 miles northwest of Anderson and roughly an hour from downtown Indianapolis via Anderson and I-69.
cities.character: Frankton is a small town in northern Madison County, about 12 miles northwest of Anderson, with SR-128 running straight through its center and Pipe Creek crossing the north end. Laid out in 1853 and incorporated in 1871, it has kept a tight-knit small-town feel and is home to Frankton Junior-Senior High School in the Frankton-Lapel district. Its signature event is the annual Heritage Days Festival, held every fall since 1975. Housing runs from older homes near the town center to newer construction on the edges.
highlights: Annual Heritage Days Festival every fall since 1975
Well-regarded Frankton-Lapel schools, including Frankton Junior-Senior High
Quiet Madison County small town about 12 miles from Anderson

cities.name: Brooklyn
cities.school_district: Metropolitan School District of Martinsville (Brooklyn Elementary STEM Academy)
cities.commute: Brooklyn is about 21 miles (roughly 30 to 35 minutes) from downtown Indianapolis via SR-67 north through Mooresville, with the SR-37/I-69 corridor also close by.
cities.character: Brooklyn is a small Morgan County town in Clay and Brown townships, sitting between Mooresville and Martinsville just off State Road 67, with White Lick Creek running along its east side. It was laid out in 1854 as the railroad came through, and the surrounding area has documented Underground Railroad history. Just west of town, the Goethe Link Observatory is known for its spring daffodil gardens. Local children attend MSD of Martinsville schools, including Brooklyn Elementary STEM Academy in town, and the town has grown notably over the past decade.
highlights: Goethe Link Observatory and its spring daffodil gardens just west of town
Historic railroad town (platted 1854) zoned to MSD of Martinsville
Between Mooresville and Martinsville off SR-67, about half an hour from downtown Indianapolis

cities.name: Clermont
cities.school_district: Metropolitan School District of Wayne Township (Ben Davis schools), with a small portion in MSD of Pike Township
cities.commute: Clermont is on the west side of Indianapolis, about 10 to 12 miles (roughly 15 to 20 minutes) from downtown via US-136 (Crawfordsville Road) and I-465 to I-65/I-70.
cities.character: Clermont is a small town on the west and northwest side of Indianapolis in Marion County's Pike and Wayne townships, bordering Brownsburg to the west. Since 1970 it has been an 'included town' under Unigov — legally part of Indianapolis while keeping its own town government. It is best known as the home of Lucas Oil Raceway, a drag strip, paved oval, and road course that hosts the NHRA U.S. Nationals over Labor Day weekend. Students are served primarily by MSD of Wayne Township and Ben Davis High School. It is a small, largely built-out community with older housing, so inventory is limited — buyers here are typically drawn by the west-side location, raceway proximity, and Brownsburg and Speedway access.
highlights: Home of Lucas Oil Raceway, host of the NHRA U.S. Nationals each Labor Day weekend
Self-governing 'included town' on Indy's west side with quick US-136 / I-465 access downtown
Zoned to MSD of Wayne Township (Ben Davis), just west of Speedway and next to Brownsburg

cities.name: Prince's Lakes
cities.school_district: Nineveh-Hensley-Jackson United School Corporation (Indian Creek Schools)
cities.commute: Prince's Lakes is about 45 minutes (roughly 35 miles) from downtown Indianapolis via SR-135 north to Greenwood, then I-65.
cities.character: Prince's Lakes is a small private-lake town in rural Nineveh Township at the southern edge of Johnson County, incorporated in 1956 and named for four namesake lakes within the community. Life here centers on the water, with boating, fishing, and swimming, and East Lake as the largest body of water. The town sits near Brown County and Camp Atterbury, drawing buyers who want an affordable lakefront or cottage lifestyle within the Indianapolis metro. Homes range from modest cottages to lakefront properties with docks and water views, so waterfront lots carry a premium.
highlights: Private-lake town built around four namesake lakes with boating, fishing, and swimming
Served by Indian Creek Schools (Nineveh-Hensley-Jackson)
Affordable cottage and lakefront homes in rural south Johnson County near Brown County

cities.name: Camby
cities.school_district: Metropolitan School District of Decatur Township (Decatur Central); the far southwest / Morgan-County edge is served by Mooresville Consolidated School Corporation
cities.commute: Camby is about 25 minutes (roughly 13 to 15 miles) from downtown Indianapolis via SR-67 (Kentucky Avenue) to I-465 and I-70.
cities.character: Camby is a growing southwest-side community centered along Camby Road near State Road 67 (Kentucky Avenue) in western Decatur Township, Marion County, with edges reaching into Hendricks and Morgan counties. A historic railroad and farming settlement once known as West Union Station, it has since filled in with newer subdivisions and new-construction neighborhoods. Buyers are drawn by relatively affordable family homes, new builds, and quick access to I-465, the Indianapolis airport, Plainfield, and Mooresville. Most students attend the Metropolitan School District of Decatur Township, feeding Decatur Central High School, while the southwest edge near Mooresville is served by Mooresville schools.
highlights: Southwest-side growth corridor along SR-67 / Kentucky Avenue in Decatur Township
New-construction subdivisions and affordable family homes, Decatur Central schools
Quick access to I-465, the airport, Plainfield, and Mooresville

cities.name: Meridian Hills
cities.school_district: Metropolitan School District of Washington Township (North Central High School); one block lies in Indianapolis Public Schools
cities.commute: Meridian Hills is about 15 minutes (roughly 8 miles) from downtown Indianapolis via North Meridian Street (US-31) or Keystone Avenue.
cities.highways: North Meridian Street (US-31), Keystone Avenue, I-465
cities.character: Meridian Hills is a small, affluent incorporated town in Washington Township about 8 miles north of downtown Indianapolis, strung along the prestigious North Meridian Street corridor. A wooded residential enclave of mostly non-HOA single-family homes, it grew from early-1920s construction, incorporated in 1937, and later became an 'included town' under Unigov. The community is anchored by Meridian Hills Country Club, which opened in 1923, and sits beside Park Tudor School, one of the state's top private schools. Buyers are drawn by mature-tree estate lots, north-side prestige, and Washington Township's North Central High School.
highlights: Affluent, wooded 'included town' about 8 miles north of downtown along North Meridian Street
Home to Meridian Hills Country Club (1923) and next to Park Tudor School
Established estate homes on large, non-HOA wooded lots

cities.name: Homecroft
cities.school_district: Metropolitan School District of Perry Township (Perry Township Schools)
cities.commute: Homecroft is about 9 miles from downtown Indianapolis, roughly a 15 to 20 minute drive via Madison Avenue (former US-31) or nearby I-65.
cities.character: Homecroft is a tiny residential enclave in southern Marion County, laid out in 1923 by Frank Gates and incorporated in 1949; it became an 'included town' with its own town council and police under Indianapolis' Unigov consolidation in 1970. The town of Southport borders it directly to the south, and a large portion of Homecroft is listed on the National Register of Historic Places as the Homecroft Historic District. Housing is almost entirely early-20th-century and mid-century single-family homes on established lots, which draws buyers who want small-town identity and mature streets inside the Indianapolis city limits. It is served by Perry Township Schools (Homecroft Elementary, Southport Middle, Southport High).
highlights: Historic small-town enclave on the National Register (Homecroft Historic District)
Its own town government and police department within Indianapolis under Unigov
Established mid-century and early-1900s homes, walkable to Southport

cities.name: Coatesville
cities.school_district: Mill Creek Community School Corporation (Cascade schools, based in Clayton)
cities.commute: Coatesville is about 35 miles from downtown Indianapolis, roughly a 45-minute drive east on US-36 through Danville, connecting to I-74 and I-465.
cities.character: Coatesville is a small rural town in Clay Township on US-36 in western Hendricks County, founded in the late 1860s and incorporated in 1909. Its defining historical event was the Good Friday tornado of March 26, 1948, which destroyed much of the town; the community rebuilt and today keeps landmarks like the Coatesville-Clay Township Public Library. It sits on the far western edge of the Indianapolis metro, offering an affordable, country setting with older homes and acreage, and is served by the Cascade schools of Mill Creek Community School Corporation. Buyers here are typically drawn by low prices, small-town quiet, and rural land rather than by a large active market.
highlights: Affordable, rural western-Hendricks town with acreage options
Cascade schools (Mill Creek Community School Corporation) in nearby Clayton
Small, thin housing market on the far-west edge of the metro
